weeks.title: Holiness Is God’s Will
weeks.theme: Holiness is not a list of prohibitions; it is how people who belong to God live out love in an honorable way.
group: Read 1 Thess 4:3–4. What picture do the words “holiness” and “honor” give you?
What has been your impression of sexual purity before marriage: fear, shame, or hope? Why?
This week, set one boundary of your own and ask a partner to hold you accountable. What is your first step?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, say one sentence to a spiritual partner of the same sex: “I want to honor God with holiness and dignity in my body and in my relationships. Please pray for me.” Then send one sentence to a friend: You are precious, and loved by God.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, make an “honor agreement”: with a partner, write down three boundaries of your own (for example, not being alone late at night, not looking at images that tempt me, only meeting on dates in public places), and agree to check in once a week. The boundaries are set by you and are for the sake of love, not for shaming.

lessons.title: It Is God’s Will That You Be Holy
lessons.hear:
When some people hear the word holiness, their first reaction is tension: are we being told again what we can’t do? Xiaohui grew up in the church and heard many warnings, but no one ever told her what holiness is for, so she always felt that holiness meant God was afraid of us being happy.

Paul writes, “For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality.” (1 Thess 4:3) Notice that he speaks first of God’s will, God’s heart toward us: to be sanctified is to be set apart for God, to belong to God. Then he says to “know how to control his own body in sanctification and honor.” (1 Thess 4:4) Holiness comes with honor; it is not suppression, but knowing that you are precious and therefore not handing yourself over carelessly.

The starting point of holiness is first being loved by God and belonging to God. We are not loved in exchange for making no mistakes; because we are already loved, we want to live with honor.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was holy, yet he drew near to people and did not reject sinners. The Bible is my standard: it is God’s will that you be holy. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing, and he makes me able. The life of self treats holiness as a performance; the selfless life, because it belongs to God, wants to live with honor.
think: According to 1 Thess 4:3, what is God’s will?
In the past, has my feeling about holiness been shame, fear, or honor?
How can I treat my body in an honorable way today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for loving me and making me yours. Renew my view of holiness, so that I no longer see it as a burden but see its honor. Holy Spirit, guide me to live in my body and relationships in the way that pleases you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, do one small thing that honors yourself: tidy your appearance, eat a good meal, or say no to a request that makes you uncomfortable. In the evening, write one sentence: I belong to God.
lessons.quick: Holiness is not being forbidden; it is belonging to God and living with honor.
text: For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality,
that each one of you know how to control his own body in sanctification and honor,
not in the passion of lust, even as the Gentiles who don’t know God,

lessons.title: Flee Sexual Immorality
lessons.hear:
Jie said, “I’ve tried hard not to think about it, but the more I suppress it, the more I think about it.” His problem is not that he isn’t trying hard enough; it is that the method is wrong.

The word Paul uses is interesting: “Flee sexual immorality!” (1 Cor 6:18) He doesn’t say resist, he doesn’t say endure; he says flee. Joseph did exactly this, and we will see it next week. Some temptations cannot be faced by standing firm; they can only be avoided by leaving.

Paul then gives the reason: “he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.” (1 Cor 6:18) This line reminds us that sex is not a trivial matter; it involves the whole person, including body, soul, and relationships.

Fleeing is not weakness but wisdom. And it is not done alone: leave that situation, find a partner, and tell what is happening.

If your body has ever been violated, that is not your sin, and it is not that you failed to flee well. Let this passage be words that protect you, not words that condemn you; and seek professional help and trusted partners.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in temptation he left, and he answered with God’s word. The Bible is my standard: flee sexual immorality. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me when I need to leave. The life of self says, “I can handle it,” and sinks deeper; the selfless life humbly admits its weakness and chooses to flee, and to ask for help.
think: Which verb does Paul use in 1 Cor 6:18?
How have I dealt with temptation in the past: by gritting my teeth, ignoring it, or leaving and asking for help?
Which situation where I easily fall can I leave first today?
lessons.speak: Lord, I admit that I often think I can hold out by myself. Give me a humble heart that knows its own weakness, to leave early and ask for help early. Heal also those who have been violated, so that they know it is not their sin. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, identify one situation that easily makes you fall (a time, a place, a person, a website), write down how you will leave it, and tell a partner this sentence.
lessons.quick: Some temptations are overcome not by standing firm but by leaving, and do not flee alone.
text: Flee sexual immorality! “Every sin that a man does is outside the body,” but he who commits sexual immorality sins against his own body.
Or don’t you know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God? You are not your own,
for you were bought with a price. Therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are God’s.

lessons.title: How Can a Young Person Keep His Way Pure?
lessons.hear:
Xiaojie, who is twenty-five, asked, “I know I should be pure, but how can I do it?” This is actually a very ancient question; the psalmist asked it three thousand years ago: “How can a young man keep his way pure?” (Ps 119:9) The answer is to live according to God’s word.

The psalmist’s answer is not greater willpower, but God’s word. Purity is not produced by gritting your teeth; it comes from being washed and guided by God’s word again and again. So to hold on to purity, put God’s word into daily life: read it, memorize it, meditate on it, compare yourself against it, and speak it aloud when temptation comes.

God’s word is also not a knife used only to point out mistakes; it is also a lamp and food, giving us strength for the next step.

“Young” refers to anyone who is building the direction of life, regardless of age. If you feel it is already too late, this passage still welcomes you, and you can start again today.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he overcame temptation with God’s word. The Bible is my standard: cleanse my way by living according to God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he puts the word into my heart. Live from the heart and rely on the Spirit, not on the mind and on self; putting God’s word into my heart is more powerful than gritting my teeth. God’s word is a lamp, and it is also strength.
think: According to Ps 119:9, how does a young person keep his way pure?
Are reading Scripture and meditating on it part of my daily life right now?
Which verse can I choose today to place at the moment when I most easily fall?
lessons.speak: Lord, I often try to live a clean life by my own strength, and I often fail. Cleanse me with your word, make me love your word and be willing to obey it. Holy Spirit, put your word in my heart so that I remember it when I need it. Amen.
lessons.do: Choose a verse about purity (such as Ps 119:9 or 1 Cor 6:18), copy it onto a sticky note, put it on the back of your phone or in front of your desk, and read it aloud three times today.
lessons.quick: Purity is not produced by gritting your teeth; it is washed clean by God’s word.
text: How can a young man keep his way pure? By living according to your word.

lessons.title: Treat the Younger Women as Sisters
lessons.hear:
Akai said, “I don’t want to be too cold toward the opposite sex, and I don’t want to be misunderstood. How exactly should I relate to them?” Paul’s advice to Timothy is interesting: “the younger as sisters, in all purity.” (1 Tim 5:2)

This verse raises a key point: in God’s household, we are not potential candidates; we are brothers and sisters. Treating people as sisters and brothers is respect, and it is also protection: it sees the other person as a whole person, with a family, a calling, and dignity, and not only looks or possibilities.

Paul also says “in all purity,” meaning that both behavior and motives are transparent. In practice, you can start with habits like these: interact in groups, avoid being alone late at night, stay transparent with others, and don’t send ambiguous messages.

This is not being unfriendly; it is loving people with a pure heart. On the other hand, when someone does not respect your boundaries, you can say so plainly, and you can leave.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he respected every person, and was pure. The Bible is my standard: treat people as brothers and sisters, in all purity. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he keeps my gaze and my motives clean. People matter more than things, and relationships matter more than possessions; treat people as people, not as targets.
think: What does 1 Tim 5:2 call the younger women we are to treat well?
Is my attitude toward friends of the opposite sex distant, ambiguous, or pure and friendly?
How can I treat a person of the opposite sex today with the heart of a brother or sister?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for teaching me to treat everyone as a brother or sister. Cleanse my gaze and my motives, so that I am pure before people. Give me wisdom, too, to say no clearly when needed, and to respect other people’s boundaries. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, show a “brother-and-sister style” of care to a friend of the opposite sex: ask how he or she is doing in a group setting, and avoid a private, ambiguous tone or late-night messages.
lessons.quick: Treating people as brothers and sisters is respect, and it is also protection.
text: the elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, in all purity.

lessons.title: Now You Have Been Washed, Sanctified
lessons.hear:
This week we talked about holiness: God’s will, fleeing sexual immorality, God’s word, and treating others as sisters. By this point, many people have a heavy voice in their hearts: “It’s already too late. What I did in the past can’t be undone.”

In 1 Cor 6:11, Paul first lists a series of unrighteous people, then writes: “Some of you were such, but you were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.” (1 Cor 6:11) The “now” here is the gospel: not because you have become good, but because Christ’s blood has washed you.

If your past includes falling, you can bring it before God today, without hiding. If your past is of being hurt, that is not your sin, you don’t need to carry shame for it, and you need to be accompanied and to have professional help.

Looking back on this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, he cleanses me; the Bible is my standard, God’s will is that we be holy; the Holy Spirit is my guide, he makes me holy. The life of self tries to make itself clean; the selfless life relies on Christ’s washing. Let Jesus be King, and give all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God hold me up this week through his word and his grace?
Which shame from my past am I willing to hand over to Christ to be washed?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for washing me and declaring me righteous. I hand over to you my past, my shame, and my weakness; set me free. Heal those who have been hurt, and let all of us know that we belong to you. Glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: this week’s discoveries, one boundary I am willing to set, and one thing I am willing to say out loud; and send this sentence to a partner: I am a person who has been washed and loved.
lessons.quick: I am washed by Christ and loved by God, and I can start again today.
text: Some of you were such, but you were washed. You were sanctified. You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and in the Spirit of our God.

weeks.keyText: For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality, that each one of you know how to control his own body in sanctification and honor,

weeks.title: Guarding Your Heart and Your Boundaries
weeks.theme: A boundary is not a cold wall but a guardrail of love; with a partner who holds you accountable, you don’t have to keep it alone.
group: Read Prov 4:23. Which entrance of your heart most needs guarding: your eyes, your ears, your mouth, or your time?
Is there a boundary you set for yourself that you keep being pushed to give up? Who pushes, and in what situations?
Which partner do you want to invite to hold each other accountable this week? What do you want to ask him or her to ask you?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, find a trustworthy partner and say: “Please ask me once a week how I am doing at keeping my boundaries.” Then send one sentence to a friend: May you have wise people walking with you, and a pure heart.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, meet with two or three partners. Each person shares one boundary and the hardest moment to keep it, and you pray for one another. If someone shares an experience of having a boundary crossed or being forced, listen seriously without judging, and accompany him or her in seeking professional help.

lessons.title: Guard Your Heart, and Put Away Lying Lips
lessons.hear:
Xiaofang had grown close to a brother. He messaged her every day, and although she clearly felt uncomfortable, she told her friends, “It’s nothing, just an ordinary friend.” She also told that brother, “I really like chatting like this.” Neither was the truth.

Proverbs says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life. Put away from yourself a perverse mouth.” (Prov 4:23–24) It is no coincidence that guarding the heart and removing lies are placed together: when the heart is not honest, the mouth speaks falsehood; and when the mouth speaks falsehood, the heart sees itself even less clearly.

The first step of a boundary is to be honest with yourself, with God, and with the other person: what I want, what I don’t want, and what I can do. Telling the truth is not coldness; it gives love a real place to stand firm. An honest refusal is better than a people-pleasing acceptance.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he said yes when it was yes and no when it was no. The Bible is my standard: guard your heart, and put away a perverse mouth. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he enables me to speak in truth. The life of self pleases others and deceives itself; the selfless life is honest in Christ. Honesty is the foundation of love.
think: What does it mean that Prov 4:23–24 puts the “heart” and the “mouth” together?
In what matter have I recently not told the truth to myself or to the other person?
What honest but gentle sentence can I say today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, make my heart honest, and keep my mouth from speaking falsehood. I often say things against my own heart so as not to disappoint people. Give me courage to speak in truth, and to speak in love. Amen. And make every word I say true.
lessons.do: Today, pick one small thing you have never dared to say, and say it with one honest and gentle sentence, for example: “I need to think about it. I’ll get back to you later.”
lessons.quick: An honest boundary is the first step of love.
text: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.
Put away from yourself a perverse mouth. Put corrupt lips far from you.

lessons.title: Joseph Runs Away
lessons.hear:
Joseph managed everything in Potiphar’s house. His master’s wife spoke to him every day, trying to seduce him. He refused again and again, and said that this would be sinning against God. One day, when no one else was in the house, she caught him by his garment and told him to lie with her.

The Bible records: “He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.” (Gen 39:12) He didn’t stay to argue, and he didn’t try to test how strong his willpower was; he fled. He would rather lose his coat than lose his purity.

This passage is often used to teach men and women, but there is another layer in it: Joseph was someone being harassed by a person in power. Being harassed was not his fault; there was no shame in his running away. If you were ever forced to give way, remember that running away and asking for help are both wise and brave choices.

Sometimes a boundary is a sentence; sometimes it is a door, a turn of the body.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he left before temptation, and he also left before danger. The Bible is my standard: Joseph left his garment and ran outside. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me when it is time to go. The life of self thinks it can handle things; the selfless life humbly leaves, and also seeks help.
think: In Gen 39:12, what did Joseph do when he met temptation?
Have I ever stayed “a little longer” and then found out it was already too late?
Can I decide in advance today which kind of situation I will leave?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for preparing a way out for me. Keep me from overestimating myself, and help me leave early when it is time to go. Protect also those who have been harassed, so that they know running away and asking for help are permitted. Amen. And keep my steps.
lessons.do: Today, set a “leave signal” for yourself: in which kind of situation (for example, a late-night invitation to be alone, or being pressured to drink) you will leave right away or call a partner; and tell a partner about this signal.
lessons.quick: Leaving when it is time to leave is wisdom, and it is courage.
text: She caught him by his garment, saying, “Lie with me!” He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside.

lessons.title: Watch and Pray, So You Don’t Enter into Temptation
lessons.hear:
In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus said to the three disciples, “Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” (Matt 26:41) This was Jesus’ last charge to them before he was arrested. Peter had just said he was ready to die with him, and in a moment he was asleep.

Acheng felt strongly about this verse. He said, “I made up my mind never to look at certain things again. I’m strong all day, but when late at night comes, I’m especially weak.” Jesus spoke very gently: the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak. He did not scold Peter, but he did not say that weakness doesn’t matter either. He said: watch and pray.

To watch is to know your most vulnerable moments and prepare ahead; to pray is to hand yourself over to the Lord who is stronger than I am. The two go together, relying not on willpower but on dependence.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in his weakest night, he was praying. The Bible is my standard: watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps my weak heart. The life of self relies on determination; the selfless life relies on dependence. Humbly admitting weakness is the starting point of victory.
think: According to Matt 26:41, what must I do so as not to enter into temptation?
In which part of the day am I weakest?
How can I “watch and pray” during that time?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, my spirit is willing, but my flesh is weak. Have mercy on me, so that I neither pretend to be strong nor give up. Teach me, in my weakest moments, to watch and pray and hand myself over to you. Amen. And hold me up, so that I do not lose heart in my weakness.
lessons.do: Find the time of day when you are most easily weak. Today, before that time, set a reminder that says: Watch and pray. When the time comes, stop and pray for one minute.
lessons.quick: Admitting weakness, watching and praying, is the starting point of victory.
text: Watch and pray, that you don’t enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”

lessons.title: Not Even Mentioned
lessons.hear:
Once Xiaoyu was chatting with friends, and everyone started making jokes with sexual innuendo. He felt uncomfortable inside but laughed along. When he got home he felt a bit upset: “It’s just a joke. Is it really that serious?”

Paul says, “But sexual immorality, and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be mentioned among you, as becomes saints.” (Eph 5:3) This is a heavy statement, but it is not meant to make us stiff and old-fashioned; it reminds us that words shape thoughts, and thoughts affect actions.

Boundaries also include what we are willing to listen to, laugh at, and forward. In friendship, you can choose not to join in, you can change the subject, and you can say gently, “I don’t want to talk about this.”

If you are offended by other people’s words, or forced to listen to vulgar talk, that is not your problem. You can leave, and you can ask someone you trust for help.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his words make people clean. The Bible is my standard: sexual immorality and all uncleanness should not even be mentioned among the saints. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me which words I should not say or listen to. The life of self goes with the flow in order to fit in; the selfless life still belongs to Christ in the crowd.
think: Which things does Eph 5:3 say should not even be mentioned?
In what kind of setting have I recently not said no because I feared awkwardness?
How can I state my boundary in a gentle way today?
lessons.speak: Lord, guard my ears, my eyes, and my lips. I often go along with unsuitable topics in order to fit in. Give me courage and wisdom to state my boundary with gentle words, without hurting anyone. Amen. And let my eyes and my tongue belong wholly to you.
lessons.do: Today, when you meet an unsuitable joke, try saying one gentle sentence: “I’m not too comfortable with this. Let’s talk about something else.” If it is hard to speak up, tell a partner afterward.
lessons.quick: Words shape thoughts; boundaries include what I am willing to listen to and laugh at.
text: But sexual immorality, and all uncleanness or covetousness, let it not even be mentioned among you, as becomes saints;

lessons.title: Walk with the Wise
lessons.hear:
This week we talked about guarding the heart, Joseph running away, watching and praying, and boundaries in speech. The last question is: you don’t need to keep it alone.

Aen said, “I tried many times to resolve on my own, and failed every time. Then a brother started asking me every week, ‘How are you doing at keeping it?’ His question was more powerful than my determination.”

Proverbs says, “One who walks with wise men grows wise,” (Prov 13:20) while a companion of fools suffers harm. The people we walk with shape us. Find a partner who is godly, honest, and does not humiliate people, and hold each other accountable; this is not surveillance but supporting one another.

Also beware: if someone, in the name of love, monitors your phone, restricts your friends, or tells you not to tell anyone, that is not walking together but control, and you deserve a safer relationship.

Looking back on this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in it?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, he watched and prayed; the Bible is my standard, guard your heart; the Holy Spirit is my guide, he makes me honest and watchful. The life of self tries to keep guard alone; the selfless life walks with the wise. Let Jesus be King, and give all glory to God. One person cannot hold the line alone, but two walking together have strength.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God hold me up this week through a partner or through Scripture?
Which person am I willing to invite to hold each other accountable with me?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for letting me not have to keep it alone. Give me wise people to walk with, so that we support one another and do not control one another. Make me honest in speaking of my weakness, and protect me from any control in the name of love. Glory to you. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, message a partner you trust and invite him or her to hold each other accountable: “Please ask me one question every week.” And agree on the time of your first conversation.
lessons.quick: The people we walk with shape us; choose to walk with the wise, not with someone who controls you.
text: One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm.

weeks.keyText: Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.

weeks.title: After You Fall
weeks.theme: Falling is not the end; God waits to cleanse us at the place of confession, and in true repentance we begin again.
group: Read 1 John 1:9. Between “confess” and “cleanse,” what does God do?
After you fell in the past, was your habit to hide, to blame yourself, or to come into the light?
To which trustworthy person are you willing to openly tell something you have been hiding this week?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, say one sentence to a trusted pastor or partner: “I have fallen, and I need you to walk with me for a while.” The listener says only: “Thank you for telling me. Let’s pray together.” Then send one sentence to a friend: God’s grace is sufficient for you.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, arrange a “conversation in the light”: sit down alone with a trusted pastor or partner and say out loud something you have been hiding. The other person only needs to listen and pray, without judging and without telling anyone else. If the matter involves being hurt or forced, please seek professional counseling.

lessons.title: If We Confess Our Sins
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqi fell. In a relationship she crossed her own boundary, and afterward she sank into shame, afraid to pray and afraid to go to church. She thought, “God must be so disappointed. I don’t deserve to go back.”

John writes, “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) This verse does not say, “First become good”; it says you only need to confess. God is faithful, because he keeps his promise; he is righteous, because Christ has already borne the price of sin.

Confession is not self-torture; it is returning to the light and telling the truth about what happened. Shame makes people hide; grace makes people come out.

If your fall was actually a case of being forced or used by someone, that is not your sin. You don’t need to confess it; please let people protect you first, and seek professional help.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he welcomed the repentant and sat at the table with sinners. The Bible is my standard: if we confess our sins, God will forgive and cleanse us. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing to return to the light. The life of self hides, defends, or blames itself; the selfless life humbly confesses and receives cleansing.
think: According to 1 John 1:9, what does God do after we confess?
After I fall, is my habitual reaction to hide, to defend myself, or to blame myself?
What is one thing I can say to God today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I come before you and tell you about my fall, no longer hiding. According to your faithfulness and righteousness, forgive me and cleanse me. Keep me from living in shame any longer, and let me live in your grace. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, find a quiet place and write on a piece of paper the thing you least dare to say, confess it to God, and then write underneath: God is faithful and righteous, and he will forgive me. Then tear up the paper or burn it.
lessons.quick: Confession is not being judged; it is returning to the light to receive cleansing.
text: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

lessons.title: Create in Me a Clean Heart, O God
lessons.hear:
David committed a grave sin, and only when the prophet Nathan came to him did David wake up. Psalm 51 is his prayer of repentance. He did not defend himself or push the responsibility onto others. He said, “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (Ps 51:10)

Notice that what David asks for is not only to be forgiven, but to be renewed: a clean heart, a right spirit. He knew the problem was not only in behavior but in the heart; behavior can stop, but the heart needs God to create it.

If you are afraid because you have fallen, remember: God is the God who creates; he doesn’t only want you to stop sinning, he is willing to create a new heart for you.

Repentance is not making more amends; it is asking God for renewal, and being willing to change the ways in your life where you easily fall.

You can take this sentence as your own prayer today and read it slowly.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he sent the Spirit so that people have a new heart. The Bible is my standard: create in me a clean heart, O God. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he renews me within. The life of self works hard at remaking itself; the selfless life asks God to create a new heart. What God renews is not only behavior but, above all, the heart.
think: In Ps 51:10, what is David asking for?
Do I want only to stop sinning, or do I want a new heart?
How can I ask God for this new heart today?
lessons.speak: God, create in me a clean heart, and renew a right spirit within me. I don’t only want to stop sinning; I want to be renewed by you. Take away my pride and shame, and let me live in your light. Amen. And let me live before you every day.
lessons.do: Today, pray Ps 51:10 as a prayer and read it three times. Then pick one habit that makes you stumble, and write down one concrete way you are willing to adjust it.
lessons.quick: Repentance is not only stopping; it is asking God to renew my heart.
text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

lessons.title: Neither Do I Condemn You
lessons.hear:
A crowd brought a woman who had been caught to Jesus, wanting to stone her to death. Jesus bent down and wrote on the ground, asking them to look at themselves first, and the people left one by one, until only Jesus and the woman remained.

Then Jesus said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?” She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:10–11)

The two sentences must be held together: “Neither do I condemn you” is grace; “From now on, sin no more” is truth. What Jesus gave first was no condemnation, and only then did he say, go. Grace comes before change, not after it.

This passage also reminds us not to throw stones at those who have fallen in the church. If someone is humiliated, that is not Jesus’ way.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he holds grace and truth together, first not condemning, then calling to new life. The Bible is my standard: neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lets me receive grace and also gives me strength to leave sin. The life of self is either a condemner or self-condemning; the selfless life receives grace from Jesus.
think: What two things did Jesus say to the woman in John 8:10–11?
In the past, have I been more ready to condemn myself or to condemn others?
How can I hold grace and truth together today?
lessons.speak: Jesus, thank you for not condemning me. Let me receive your grace, and no longer throw stones at myself or at others. Holy Spirit, give me strength to obey what you said: go, and sin no more. Amen. And teach me to see those who have fallen through your eyes.
lessons.do: Today, when you are about to speak to yourself with a self-blaming sentence, say instead: Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you.” Also, at church or among friends, say one encouraging, non-condemning sentence to someone who has fallen.
lessons.quick: Jesus first does not condemn, then calls to new life.
text: Jesus, standing up, saw her and said, “Woman, where are your accusers? Did no one condemn you?”
She said, “No one, Lord.” Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.”

lessons.title: Whoever Conceals His Sins Will Not Prosper
lessons.hear:
Axuan had a secret he had hidden for three years. He and a former girlfriend had crossed the line, but he had never told anyone. He said, “Every time I go into church, I feel like a fake.”

Proverbs says, “He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.” (Prov 28:13) Concealing keeps our lives from flowing, and there is always a layer between us and our hearts. When we confess and forsake, God shows mercy. Notice that there are two actions here: confessing is returning to the light; forsaking is turning around.

Confessing doesn’t require telling the details in front of everyone. You can tell God first, and then slowly tell a trusted pastor or counselor. What matters is that you no longer carry it alone.

If your secret involves someone else’s harm or coercion, please make sure you are safe first, and seek professional help.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he welcomes those who are honest, and he protects those who have been hurt. The Bible is my standard: whoever confesses and renounces sins finds mercy. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me willing to tell the truth. The life of self conceals and packages; the selfless life is honest and accepts help. In the light there is no shame, only mercy.
think: According to Prov 28:13, what happens to the one who conceals his sins? And to the one who confesses and renounces them?
Is there something in my heart right now that I have kept hidden?
To which trustworthy person can I choose to say it?
lessons.speak: Lord, I admit that I often choose to conceal because I am afraid of being looked down on. Give me courage to confess to you and to be honest with someone I trust. Help me forsake my sin and receive your mercy. Amen. And walk with me out of the days of hiding.
lessons.do: Today, pick a trusted pastor or counselor and send a message to schedule a conversation. The message only needs to say: “There’s something I’d like to talk with you about. When would be convenient for you?”
lessons.quick: Confessing is returning to the light; forsaking is turning around.
text: He who conceals his sins doesn’t prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy.

lessons.title: I Acknowledged My Sin
lessons.hear:
Psalm 32 was written by David after he repented. He first describes the days when he did not confess and stayed silent: his body was weary, his heart was heavy, as if his bones were drying up.

Then he writes the turning point: “I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my transgressions to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.” (Ps 32:5) With one act, the burden pressing on him was lifted.

This week we have walked from 1 John 1:9 to Psalm 32, and the final answer is the same: return to the light and receive forgiveness.

What he chose was not to try harder but to be more honest: he laid everything out before God, and forgiveness came.

Looking back on this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in it? Whether today you are the one who fell, or the one accompanying someone who fell, remember: grace is greater than our shame.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, he does not condemn and he calls to new life; the Bible is my standard, those who confess will be forgiven; the Holy Spirit is my guide, he creates a clean heart. The life of self hides and blames itself; the selfless life hands everything over to God. Let Jesus be King, and give all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God hold me up in it?
To whom do I need to confess, or to whom do I need to extend a hand of grace?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for your forgiveness and cleansing. I hand over to you my hiding and my shame; make me free again. Make me also someone who extends grace to those who have fallen. Glory to you. Amen. And teach me to extend a hand of grace.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week, one thing I need to confess to God or to someone, and find a partner to pray for this matter.
lessons.quick: Confession lifts the burden, and grace is greater than shame.
text: I acknowledged my sin to you. I didn’t hide my iniquity. I said, I will confess my transgressions to the LORD, and you forgave the iniquity of my sin. Selah.

weeks.keyText: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

weeks.title: Guarding Your Eyes and Heart
weeks.theme: The eyes are the window of the heart; we guard what we look at so that the whole person may live in the light, not in shame.
group: Read Ps 119:37. What is the “vanity” that most needs to be turned away from in your life?
At what time of day, and with what device, do you most often find yourself looking, without meaning to, at things you don’t want to look at?
What boundary are you willing to set for your eyes this week? Whom will you ask to check in with you?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, say to a partner of the same sex: “I want to make a covenant with my eyes. Please ask me about it once a week.” Then send one sentence to a friend: May your eyes be clear, and your whole body full of light.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, keep an “eyes’ Sabbath”: choose half a day with no social media and no videos, and instead take a walk, read Scripture, and see friends. Afterward write down: What did I look at less? What did I see more?

lessons.title: Turn Away My Eyes from Looking at Vanity
lessons.hear:
Every night before bed, Xiaozhe scrolled on his phone for an hour. It seemed casual, but the more he looked, the emptier he felt: who was living better, who was better looking, who had posted another sweet couple photo. Some images made him envious, some made him discouraged, and some he knew he shouldn’t look at.

The psalmist prays, “Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.” (Ps 119:37) Notice that he says “turn away my eyes”: he knows he cannot turn them by himself and needs God’s help. Vanity is what looks very real but cannot bring life: edited lives, commodified bodies, magnified comparisons.

To turn the eyes is not only to stop looking but to turn toward: toward God’s way, toward real people, toward a life-giving life. Turning the eyes does not come from deciding once; it is adjusting direction every day.

You can try it once tonight.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his eyes were fixed on what the Father was doing. The Bible is my standard: turn away my eyes from vanity, and live in God’s way. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me turn my eyes. The life of self tries to control its eyes by willpower; the selfless life prays, “Turn away my eyes.” God’s word is a lamp to my feet.
think: In Ps 119:37, what does the psalmist ask of God?
What “vanity” most often catches my eyes?
To what real and life-giving thing can I turn my eyes today?
lessons.speak: Lord, turn away my eyes from looking at vanity, and revive me in your ways. I admit that I often linger where I shouldn’t look. Have mercy on me, and help me turn toward what is real, toward you. Amen. And be with me tonight.
lessons.do: Tonight before bed, put your phone on the charger in the living room, and instead read a psalm and write one sentence of thanks. If you can’t do it, tell a partner.
lessons.quick: Turning the eyes is not only not looking; it is turning toward real life.
text: Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.

lessons.title: I Made a Covenant with My Eyes
lessons.hear:
Job was an upright man, and he left a very special record about his life: “I made a covenant with my eyes. How then should I look lustfully at a young woman?” (Job 31:1) He did not rely on willpower to hold out when it happened; he made a covenant beforehand: I decide where my eyes will not go.

A covenant has several features: it is made beforehand, it is clear, and it is voluntary. Many people fail because they decide what to do only at the moment temptation arrives, when it is hardest. Job’s way was to set his direction in ordinary, clear-headed times.

You can also make a covenant for your eyes: write down concrete rules, such as what times you won’t scroll your phone, which websites you won’t open, and which kind of image you will close immediately. Then find a partner, so that this covenant is not known only to you.

Making a covenant is not for self-blame but for protection, so that love has room.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his eyes were full of compassion, and also simply focused. The Bible is my standard: I made a covenant with my eyes. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me keep the covenant. The life of self relies on a last-minute resolve; the selfless life sets the covenant first, in peace, and lets others walk with it. The covenant is set first, and then peace remains.
think: In Job 31:1, how did Job treat his eyes?
Have I ever set clear rules in advance for my eyes or my phone?
Which rule am I willing to write down today, and whom will I tell?
lessons.speak: God, you know that my eyes often don’t listen to me. Help me make a covenant with my eyes, so that I decide my direction first, while I am at peace. Give me strength, and give me people to walk with, so that I do not keep the covenant alone. Amen. And do not let me be alone.
lessons.do: Today, write down three items for “my covenant with my eyes,” for example: no phone before bed, not opening a certain kind of website, closing inappropriate images immediately. Send them to a partner and ask him or her to check in with you every week.
lessons.quick: A covenant is made beforehand, made concrete, and made with someone walking alongside.
text: “I made a covenant with my eyes; how then should I look lustfully at a young woman?

lessons.title: If Your Eye Is Sound
lessons.hear:
Jesus said, “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matt 6:22–23) This passage is placed between money and anxiety, and it means that what we look at and fix our gaze on determines whether our inner life is bright or dark.

The eye is a channel, not the main character. If the eyes are occupied by vanity, comparison, and lust, the whole person is pulled toward darkness; if the eyes focus on God’s goodness, the whole person is lit up.

Xiaoyu noticed that every time she spent a while looking at other people’s perfect lives, she became more dissatisfied with her own. She began each morning by looking at three things she was grateful for before opening her phone. She said, “The light in my whole self is different.”
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he is the light of the world, and he opens people’s eyes. The Bible is my standard: the lamp of the body is the eye. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes my eyes clear. The focus is on Jesus, not on myself, not on others, not on circumstances; when my eyes see him, my whole body is full of light.
think: According to Matt 6:22–23, how are the eye and the whole body related?
What have I been looking at lately that makes my heart brighter, and what makes it darker?
Where can I put my eyes first today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the light of the world. Make my eyes clear, and put light in my heart. Forgive me for letting vanity and comparison occupy my eyes, so that I see your goodness and focus on you. Amen. And light a lamp in my dark places.
lessons.do: This morning, first spend three minutes looking at one beautiful thing (the sky, a flower, a verse), say a word of thanks, and then open your phone.
lessons.quick: When the eyes focus on the light, the whole body is full of light.
text: “The lamp of the body is the eye. If therefore your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light.
But if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!

lessons.title: David Saw a Woman
lessons.hear:
Second Samuel 11 is one of the heaviest passages in the Bible. At the height of his power, David should have gone out with his army, but he stayed in the palace. One day, “David arose from his bed, and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing.” (2 Sam 11:2) He inquired about her and sent for her, and what happened next left one person harmed and another dead.

This began with a “look,” but it was more than a look. The real turning point was David’s power: he was the king, and she had no room to say no. The Bible does not say that Bathsheba sinned; she was someone harmed in an unequal power relationship.

This passage warns us that eyes that are not restrained, combined with power, silence, and no accountability, will hurt people. It reminds both men and women not to treat the people they see as objects to take; and it reminds those who were harmed that it was not your fault.

Guarding the eyes is also guarding other people’s dignity.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his eyes saw people and gave them dignity. The Bible is my standard: after I see, I must choose how to respond. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me that every person is made by God. The life of self treats the eyes as a right; the selfless life uses the eyes to honor people.
think: In 2 Sam 11:2, what did David do first?
Have I treated people I see as objects I can take?
How can I use my eyes today to honor a person?
lessons.speak: Lord, guard my eyes and my heart, so that I do not treat anyone as someone I want to get. Heal those who have been harmed by power, so that they know it was not their fault. Let me see the dignity of every person. Amen.
lessons.do: Today, when you meet someone whose appearance you easily notice, pray for him or her in your heart, blessing the whole person, including his or her family, life, and dreams.
lessons.quick: Guarding the eyes is also guarding other people’s dignity.
text: At evening, David arose from his bed and walked on the roof of the king’s house. From the roof, he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very beautiful to look at.
David sent and inquired after the woman. One said, “Isn’t this Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam, Uriah the Hittite’s wife?”
David sent messengers, and took her; and she came in to him, and he lay with her (for she was purified from her uncleanness); and she returned to her house.

lessons.title: Whatever Things Are True, Whatever Things Are Honorable
lessons.hear:
This week we talked about turning the eyes, making a covenant, bright eyes, and we also saw David’s failure. But not looking is not enough; the eyes need somewhere to go, and the mind needs something to think about.

Paul gives a positive list: “whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report.” (Phil 4:8) These are what we are to think about. A fence can only keep out what is outside; thinking on these things can fill what is inside.

You can deliberately build a “good eyes” habit: each day read a passage of Scripture, listen to a hymn, look at one true and beautiful thing, and talk with a godly friend. When the mind is occupied by good things, there is no room for vanity.

Looking back on this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in it? If you have struggled with inappropriate images, you are not alone; please seek counseling or the company of a partner.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, his eyes were fixed on the Father; the Bible is my standard, the eye is the lamp of the body; the Holy Spirit is my guide, he makes me think on what is good and beautiful. The life of self tries to look a little less; the selfless life fixes its eyes on Christ. Let Jesus be King, and give all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God hold me up in it?
Which true and honorable thing am I willing to think about every day?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for this week’s illumination. Fill my eyes and my mind with what pleases you. Forgive my self-centeredness, and hold me up with your grace. Glory to you. Amen. And turn my thoughts simply toward you.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week, my covenant with my eyes, and the one thing I will think on every day; and copy out Phil 4:8 and put it where you often look.
lessons.quick: When the mind is occupied by good things, there is no room for vanity.
text: Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is anything worthy of praise, think about these things.

weeks.keyText: Turn my eyes away from looking at worthless things. Revive me in your ways.

weeks.title: Comparison, Being Left on Read, and Anxiety
weeks.theme: Anxiety is not weakness; it is an invitation to cast your burden on God. God watches over me, and I don’t have to live in someone else’s shadow.
group: Read 1 Pet 5:7. What does “casting” look like as an action? What have you most wanted to cast off lately?
When do you compare yourself with others most easily: on social media, with your friends’ relationships, or over appearance?
What concrete method will you use this week to come back to God first when you are waiting for a message that doesn’t come?
weeks.sunday: After Sunday worship, find a partner and each share the one thing that has made you most anxious lately, and pray for each other with 1 Pet 5:7. Then send one sentence to a friend: God cares for you, and you can cast your worries on him.
weeks.weekend: This weekend, set aside a “casting day”: write all your worries on paper, pray over them one by one before God, and seal them in an envelope. Then invite a friend for a walk, and talk not about dating but only about gratitude.

lessons.title: Casting All Your Worries on God
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqing sent a message. The other person had read it, but three hours passed with no reply. She began to imagine: “Does he not want to talk to me anymore? Did I say something wrong?” She checked her phone twenty times and couldn’t get anything done.

Peter writes, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Pet 5:7) The word “cast” means to throw a heavy load onto someone else. Notice the word before it is “all,” not a selected few; it includes worries that seem small and that you can’t put into words. After it comes the reason: because he cares for you. We can cast because the one receiving cares.

When we are anxious, we often want to solve it ourselves: analyzing again and again, checking again and again. Casting it on God is not neglecting it; it is putting down the burden of “I must control the outcome” and doing only the one small step I can do.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he entrusted everything to the Father. The Bible is my standard: cast all your worries on God. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he comforts my heart. The life of self wants to control the outcome itself; the selfless life casts its burden on the God who cares for me. God cares for me, and I can let go.
think: According to 1 Pet 5:7, what can we cast on God? Why?
Which outcome do I most want to control right now?
How can I hand it over to God in a concrete way today?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, I have many worries right now, and I hand them to you one by one. I admit that I badly want to control the outcome, but I cannot. Thank you for caring for me. Give me peace, so that I can focus on what you have given me to do today. Amen.
lessons.do: Today when you are anxious, take a piece of paper and write down three worries, and after each one write: I give it to you. Then pray, and do one small thing close at hand.
lessons.quick: I cast it on God, because he cares for me.
text: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

lessons.title: You Follow Me
lessons.hear:
The risen Jesus spoke some hard words to Peter by the sea, and also entrusted him with a task. Peter turned around, saw John, and asked, “Lord, what about this man?” (John 21:21) This is a reaction we all know: “You just spoke about my life, but what about his?”

Jesus answered, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.” (John 21:22) Jesus did not answer about John’s future; he turned Peter’s gaze back to Peter. It is not that he doesn’t love John, but that he is saying: each person’s path is personally led by him, and you don’t need to compare yourself with others.

This matters especially in dating: a friend got married, a classmate started dating, an ex has a new partner... these are all other people’s paths. What Jesus says to you is only one sentence: You follow me!

You can say it once today.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he did only what the Father gave him to do, and was not moved by other people’s gaze. The Bible is my standard: what is that to you? You follow me. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he pulls my gaze back to Jesus. The life of self keeps comparing; the selfless life looks only at Jesus. He wants my gaze to return to him.
think: In John 21:22, how did Jesus respond to Peter’s comparison?
Whom do I most often compare myself with? How does my heart feel afterward?
How can I focus on following Jesus today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I often look at others and compare myself with them, forgetting that you said to me: you follow me. Bring my eyes back to you, so that I rejoice in other people’s good, without envy or jealousy. Amen. And lead me on the path you have prepared for me.
lessons.do: Today, pray for someone you envy: thank God for the grace on his or her life. Then say to yourself: Jesus says to me, “You follow me.”
lessons.quick: What is another person’s path to me? I only need to follow Jesus.
text: Peter, seeing him, said to Jesus, “Lord, what about this man?”
Jesus said to him, “If I desire that he stay until I come, what is that to you? You follow me.”

lessons.title: Let Each Person Examine His Own Work
lessons.hear:
On social media, Atong saw his friends getting partners and engaged, one after another, and he began to doubt: “Is something not good enough about me?” Every day he opened his phone, and felt a little more loss.

Paul says, “But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself and not in someone else.” (Gal 6:4) To examine is to look at yourself honestly, not to blame yourself, and not to use others as the measuring stick. God gives each person a different path, timing, and gifts; if you use someone else’s path to judge your own life, you will always feel it is not enough.

Comparison has two extremes: feeling inferior, thinking you are not enough; and pride, thinking you are better than others. Both make the self the center.

To examine your own work is to ask: have I lived today the way God wants me to live? Not: am I better than others?
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he asked only for the Father’s heart, and did not compare himself with others. The Bible is my standard: let each man examine his own work. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he lights me up without shaming me. Feeling inferior and being proud are both centered on self; the selfless person takes God as the measuring stick.
think: According to Gal 6:4, what should we examine?
What standard have I been using lately to judge myself: God’s, or other people’s?
How can I examine myself honestly today without shaming myself?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, help me not to measure my life by someone else’s path. Shine your light on me, so that I see myself as I truly am, neither feeling inferior nor being proud. Make me focus on living the life you want me to live. Amen. And turn my heart toward you.
lessons.do: Today, turn off social media for an hour, and instead write down “three things I did today that were according to God’s heart,” with no comparing, just recording. If it is hard, tell a partner.
lessons.quick: Examine yourself by God’s standard, not by measuring against someone else’s path.
text: But let each man examine his own work, and then he will have reason to boast in himself, and not in someone else.

lessons.title: My Soul, Be Silent
lessons.hear:
Arui was waiting for an important answer, perhaps about a job, perhaps about a relationship. Her mind wouldn’t stop: “What if it’s this? What if it’s that?” She said, “The more I think, the more tired I get, but I can’t stop.”

The psalmist speaks to himself: “My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.” (Ps 62:5) He doesn’t tell himself to stop thinking, but speaks to his own soul: you, be still; you, wait for God alone. Hope does not come from the result, nor from the other person’s reply, but from God.

Being silent is not suppressing your emotions; it is bringing a clamoring heart to be still before God. You can practice: breathe deeply, pray slowly, and count God’s blessings one by one.

If the anxiety persists, or affects your sleep or daily life, please seek medical or counseling help; there is no shame in that.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he often withdrew to quiet places to pray. The Bible is my standard: my soul, wait in silence for God alone. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes me still. Live from the heart and rely on the Spirit, not on the mind and on self; use the mind and you worry, use the heart and you have joy. Only a quiet heart can hear God’s voice.
think: In Ps 62:5, how does the psalmist speak to his own soul?
What does my heart most often clamor about?
How can I let my heart be still for five minutes today?
lessons.speak: Lord, my heart is very noisy, thinking and worrying without stopping. I say to my soul: be silent, and wait for God alone. Make me still, and let my hope come only from you. Amen. And give me a measure of peace today.
lessons.do: Today, spend five minutes in a quiet place and slowly read Ps 62:5; with each reading, take one deep breath, and hand over to God the thing that is loudest in your heart.
lessons.quick: Hope does not come from the result; it comes from God.
text: My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.

lessons.title: Do Not Be Anxious About Tomorrow
lessons.hear:
This week we talked about worry, comparison, examining our own work, and a quiet heart. Finally, Jesus gives us a very practical invitation: “Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.” (Matt 6:34)

This does not tell us not to plan; it tells us not to carry in advance burdens that have not yet happened. Much anxiety comes from imagination: what if he doesn’t reply; what if I stay single forever; what if I chose wrong. Jesus says: today’s grace is enough for today, and tomorrow’s grace we will receive tomorrow.

Looking back on this week: Where did I see my self-centeredness? How did God hold me up in it?

Much anxiety comes from imagination, not reality; Jesus teaches us to receive only one day of grace at a time.

Tonight before bed you can say: Lord, today I did what I could, and the rest I hand over to you.
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, he entrusted tomorrow to the Father; the Bible is my standard, do not be anxious about tomorrow; the Holy Spirit is my guide, he gives peace. The life of self wants to carry all the tomorrows at once; the selfless life depends on God one day at a time. Let Jesus be King, and give all glory to God.
think: Where did I see my self-centeredness this week?
How did God hold me up in it?
Which matter of tomorrow am I willing to hand over to God first?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for each day’s grace. Today I did what I could, and the rest I hand over to you. Forgive my self-centeredness, and give me peace, so that I can sleep in comfort. Glory to you. Amen. And let all my tomorrows be in your hands.
lessons.do: In your journal write: my biggest discovery this week, one comparison I am willing to let go of, and one worry I am willing to entrust. Before bed, say one sentence: Today’s grace is enough for today.
lessons.quick: Today’s grace is enough for today; tomorrow’s grace we will receive tomorrow.
text: Therefore don’t be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Each day’s own evil is sufficient.

weeks.keyText: casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.

weeks.title: Messages, Words, and Privacy
weeks.theme: Words can be a channel of love or a knife that wounds; before you speak, ask: will this benefit the person who hears it?
group: Read Eph 4:29. What do “good words that build people up” and “corrupt speech” look like in today’s messages and posts?
Is there a message or a sentence you regretted as soon as you said it? What was in charge of your heart at the time?
What boundary do you want to set this week for your words and your privacy? Ask your group members to pray for you.
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, find a partner. Each of you say one “good word that builds people up” you want to say to someone this week, and then send that word to that person. When you get home, write “Pause for three seconds before speaking” in the Notes app on your phone.
weeks.weekend: Plan a “word experiment” for the weekend: for these two days, before you send any message, silently ask yourself once: Is this true? Will this benefit him? Is this the right time to say it? On Sunday evening, share with a partner: when did I stop, and when did I not?

lessons.title: Speak Only Words That Build Up
lessons.hear:
Xiaoqi and Zhe had just started dating. One day Zhe was slow to reply, and in the middle of the night Xiaoqi sent, “Do you think I’m annoying?” The next day she added a joke with a sting in it. Zhe read it, did not know how to respond, felt heavy all day, and even began to dread opening his phone.

Phones make words travel too fast, and make them feel too light. The Bible says, “Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.” (Eph 4:29) Notice that the standard is not “what I feel like saying” but “that it may give grace to those who hear.”

Good words that build people up are not sweet talk, and they do not mean being afraid to speak the truth. They are sincere, well timed, and helpful to the person. If Xiaoqi had simply said, “You didn’t reply, and I’m feeling a little anxious. Can we talk?” that would have been a good word.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: his words gave life and brought healing. The Bible is my standard: speak only what builds people up, so that those who hear receive grace. The Holy Spirit is my guide: before I open my mouth, he reminds me to pause. Those who live for self speak to vent; those who live in selflessness speak to build up.
think: According to Eph 4:29, what may come out of our mouths? What is the purpose?
Are the messages I have sent lately a way of venting my emotions, or of building the other person up?
Who is one person I can say a sincere and helpful word to today?
lessons.speak: Lord, guard my mouth, and guard my fingers too. When I want to lash out, help me pause, so that the words I say build people up and do not hurt them, so that those who hear receive grace, and so that in every reply I learn to be gentle and honest like you. Amen.
lessons.do: Before you send each message today, pause for three seconds and ask yourself: Will this benefit him? If not, delete it and rewrite it, or don’t send it. Then send one sincere message of thanks to someone.
lessons.quick: The standard for speaking is that those who hear receive grace.
text: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

lessons.title: Blessing and Cursing From One Mouth
lessons.hear:
Hao worshiped loudly at small group, but after the meeting he made fun of a sister’s outfit in the group chat. He said it was just a joke and meant no harm. But the sister saw it, and the next week she did not come back.

James puts it bluntly: “With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God. Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing.” (James 3:9–10) If someone truly worships God yet despises the people God made, that is a contradiction.

Every person is made in the image of God, including the person you find hard to get along with and the person who let you down. Humiliating someone, labeling them, or talking about them behind their back all treat God’s image as worthless. True worship extends to our lips, and it extends into the messages on our phones.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he never humiliated anyone, and even toward sinners he showed respect first. The Bible is my standard: people are made in the image of God and must not be cursed. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he makes our mouths and hearts agree, so that we respect people from the heart. Those who live for self see people’s flaws; those who live in selflessness see the image of God.
think: According to James 3:9–10, where is the contradiction between blessing and cursing?
Have I ever made fun of someone, labeled them, or joined others in speaking badly of them behind their back?
Today, how can I replace criticism with blessing?
lessons.speak: God, forgive me for using the same mouth to praise you and to look down on the people you made. Cleanse my lips, and let me see your image in every person. May all my words be for you, and may I still speak blessing when people are not around. Amen.
lessons.do: If you hear someone being mocked in a group or chat room today, don’t join in and don’t like the message. If you can, privately send an encouraging word to the person being talked about.
lessons.quick: Everyone bears God’s image, so do not curse them.
text: With it we bless our God and Father, and with it we curse men who are made in the image of God.
Out of the same mouth comes blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.

lessons.title: Many Words Bring Wrongdoing
lessons.hear:
Xiaowen trusted a person she had just met. In two weeks she poured out her family troubles and past wounds all at once. He was gentle at the time, but a month later the relationship ended, and she found that those words had been passed around among his friends.

Proverbs says, “In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience,” and the one who restrains his lips is wise. (Prov 10:19) This does not mean we should stay silent. It means that the more words we speak, the more likely we are to go wrong.

Privacy in dating takes wisdom. Trust is built step by step, not handed over all at once. Your story is precious. You can share a small part first, see how the other person treats it, and then decide whether to share more. Remember, too, that the other person’s private matters are not material for your conversations either.

This is not closing yourself off; it is guarding. You guard your own heart, and you guard other people’s privacy.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he knew when to speak and when to be silent. The Bible is my standard: whoever restrains his lips is wise. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me what to say and what to hold back for now. Those who live for self are in a hurry to be understood; those who live in selflessness let trust grow slowly.
think: According to Prov 10:19, what is the result of too many words?
Have I ever shared my own story too quickly with someone I did not yet know well enough?
What is the first privacy boundary I can set for myself?
lessons.speak: Lord, give me wisdom to know what to say and what to wait on. Keep me from carelessly handing over my private feelings, and from carelessly passing on other people’s private matters. May my speech be wise and my silence be wise, and in my relationships teach me to build trust slowly, according to your timing. Amen.
lessons.do: Today write down three things that are “not yet right to tell the other person,” and next to each write: when would I want to wait until, and what would I need to see, before I tell him?
lessons.quick: Trust is built step by step, not handed over all at once.
text: In the multitude of words there is no lack of disobedience, but he who restrains his lips does wisely.

lessons.title: Every Idle Word Will Be Accounted For
lessons.hear:
After an argument with his girlfriend, Jie took a screenshot of their conversation and posted it in a group chat of friends: “You be the judge.” In less than a day, more than ten people knew about their quarrel, and some even added their own embellishments. They later made up, but the wound stayed in his girlfriend’s heart, because she felt she had been put on public trial.

Jesus said, “I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.” (Matt 12:36) Idle words are those careless words that do no good. Jesus says even these must be accounted for.

This is not meant to frighten us. It is a reminder that words carry weight. Screenshots, forwarded messages, and group posts are all words. Especially when it involves someone else’s private matters, weaknesses, and wounds, ask one more question before you pass it on: Do I have the right to say this? Is it good for this person? If you are struggling, turn to a trusted pastor or counselor for help rather than putting someone on public trial in a group chat.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he covered people’s faults and did not broadcast them. The Bible is my standard: even idle words must be accounted for to God. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he reminds me to think before I pass something on, and teaches me to guard other people’s privacy. Those who live for self use words to seek approval; those who live in selflessness use words to protect relationships.
think: According to Matt 12:36, what will happen with the idle words people speak?
Have I ever forwarded, screenshotted, or discussed someone else’s private matters in a group?
Today, how can I repair an inappropriate conversation?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, forgive me for the idle words and improper retelling I have done. Show me who it is safe to confide in, and teach me to keep other people’s confidences, not exposing others just to vent. Make me a friend who helps people feel safe to speak. Amen.
lessons.do: Today go through the chat screenshots on your phone and delete the ones that should not be kept. If you have ever sent someone else’s private matter to a third party, say to the person involved or to the third party: “I should not have told you that. Please don’t pass it on.”
lessons.quick: Words must be accounted for. Before you pass something on, ask: Do I have the right to say this?
text: I tell you that every idle word that men speak, they will give account of it in the day of judgment.

lessons.title: Death and Life Are in the Power of the Tongue
lessons.hear:
Looking back on this week: good words that build up (Eph 4:29), blessing and cursing (James 3:9–10), many words (Prov 10:19), idle words that must be accounted for (Matt 12:36).

“Death and life are in the power of the tongue,” and those who love it will eat its fruit. (Prov 18:21) One sentence can make a person come alive, or make them sink. In dating, the words “I’m here” can bring comfort, while a single humiliating remark can take years to recover from.

Remember also: if the other person has put you down with words, threatened you, mocked you, or asked you to send private photos or information, that is not your fault, and it is not love. You can refuse, you can keep evidence, and you can ask for help from people you trust and from professional organizations.

Looking back on this week, is there a sentence you wish you could take back? Is there one you are glad you said?
lessons.light: This week’s 3-2-1: Jesus is my example, and his words bring life; the Bible is my standard, and words that build people up are the good words; the Holy Spirit is my guide, helping me stop before I speak and discern which words come from you. Those who live for self treat words as weapons; those who live in selflessness treat words as gifts. Let Jesus be King, so that even my messages bring all the glory to God.
think: Where did I see self this week? How did God support me in it?
According to Prov 18:21, how great is the power of the tongue?
What one specific change will I make next week for my words and my privacy?
lessons.speak: Heavenly Father, thank you for this week’s reminders. Forgive me where I have hurt people with my words, and heal my heart where I have been hurt by words. Let my tongue bring forth life, and let my messages be a blessing. All the glory be to you. Amen.
lessons.do: In your journal write: the one sentence I most want to take back this week; the one sentence I am most thankful for; the one boundary for my words I will set next week. Then say an apology or a thank-you to one person.
lessons.quick: The tongue holds the power of life and death; I choose to speak life.
text: Death and life are in the power of the tongue; those who love it will eat its fruit.

weeks.keyText: Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth, but only what is good for building others up as the need may be, that it may give grace to those who hear.

weeks.title: Time and Priorities
weeks.theme: Time is a gift from God; put God first, and everything else falls into its place.
group: Read Eph 5:15–16. In your life right now, what does “redeeming the time” look like in concrete terms?
Who and what gets most of your time in a week? Does that match what you say matters most?
This week, what stretch of time do you want to clear from your calendar for God, for yourself, or for an important person?
weeks.sunday: After the Sunday gathering, trade with a partner: “The block of time I most want to protect this week is…” Agree to ask each other again next Sunday: Did you protect it?
weeks.weekend: This weekend, first draw next week’s calendar on paper. Fill in “time alone with God,” “rest,” and “important people” first, and then fill in work and everything else. When you finish, share with a partner: which block will be hardest to protect, and why.

lessons.title: Redeeming the Time
lessons.hear:
Fang was dating, and every day she was replying to messages, going on dates, and talking things through, yet she felt more and more worn out. Her quiet time had shrunk to three minutes before bed, and she often skipped her small group during the week. She said, “I have no time. Every day is packed full. Even sitting down to a proper meal feels like a luxury.”

Paul says, “Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil.” (Eph 5:15–16) Redeeming the time does not mean filling up your calendar. It means spending your time on what really matters.

Dating is not a bad thing, but it takes up a lot of time, and it quietly squeezes out other priorities: time with God, rest, friendships, and family. A wise person first asks, What matters most to me? And then gives time to it. Where your time goes, your heart goes.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: he was busy, yet he often withdrew to lonely places to pray, and he was never led around by other people’s demands. The Bible is my standard: redeem the time, and walk as the wise do. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he helps me tell what comes first and what comes next. Those who live for self are pushed along by urgent things; those who live in selflessness follow God’s order.
think: According to Eph 5:15–16, how should the wise treat time?
Who gets most of my time in a week right now? Does this fit my values?
What is the one most important thing I can set aside time for today?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for giving me time. Teach me to tell what matters most, so that I am not led around by urgent things and other people’s expectations. Help me give my time first to you, and also to the people I should love, so that my days are not wasted. Amen.
lessons.do: Today open your calendar, find one thing you “really don’t need to attend,” and delete it or postpone it. Then write “time alone with God” in the time you saved.
lessons.quick: Where your time goes, your heart goes.
text: Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise,
redeeming the time, because the days are evil.

lessons.title: Teach Us to Count Our Days
lessons.hear:
On Ming’s thirtieth birthday, a friend asked him, “Have you thought about how you want to spend the next three years?” He froze. He was busy every day, yet he could not say where he was heading. He just followed his feelings and had a few relationships with no direction.

Moses prays in the Psalms, “So teach us to count our days,” that we may gain a heart of wisdom. (Ps 90:12) Counting our days does not mean worrying that we are getting older. It means admitting that my days are limited, so I should live wisely.

The heart of this prayer is “a heart of wisdom,” not faster results. A wise person is not pressured by age, by the gaze of peers, or by society’s timetable, but walks day by day before God. Some people have a calling first, some have a relationship first, and some stay single for a long time. Every one of these can be an honorable path before God.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: in thirty years of preparation he was neither hurried nor restless, yet he did not waste a single day. The Bible is my standard: count our days and gain a heart of wisdom. The Holy Spirit is my guide: he gives me peace within God’s timing. Those who live for self are chased by time; those who live in selflessness rest in God’s time.
think: According to Ps 90:12, what is the purpose of counting our days?
Am I anxious because of my age or because of other people’s opinions?
Can I ask God about one specific thing for this year today?
lessons.speak: Lord, teach me to count my days. I am often hurried along by my age and other people’s opinions. Give me a heart of wisdom, so that I do not panic and do not waste time. Lead me to walk in the time you have prepared for me, walking with you every day. Amen.
lessons.do: Today take ten minutes to write down “the three things I most want to accomplish with God in the coming year.” They don’t have to be about romance. When you finish, give the list to God in prayer.
lessons.quick: We count our days not to be anxious, but to gain a heart of wisdom.
text: So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.
